blocks.title: Good stone work starts **under the stone.**
body: HD Landscape installs river rock, black stone and boulders in St. Clair Shores and across Metro Detroit. A landscape rock job means clearing the bed, shaping the ground, setting a clean edge and spreading decorative stone on firm ground, so it stays where it is put.

People choose stone because it weathers slowly, so it does not need a fresh layer the way mulch does. The trade off: it adds nothing to the soil, it may run warmer than mulch in a sunny bed, and leaves still settle into it.

blocks.title: The same bed in stone or mulch.
blocks.intro: Tap through the finishes on one of our real beds. Color is a lot easier to judge on a bed than on a pile in a stone yard.

items.title: River rock
items.body: Rounded stone in soft gray and tan tones. It reads natural against brick and suits side yards, walks and strips where grass never took.

items.title: Black stone
items.body: Dark and modern, in sharp crushed stone or smooth pebbles. It sets off green plants and clipped shrubs, and it is the stone you will see most in our photos, at homes and commercial buildings alike.

items.title: Boulders
items.body: Set partly into the ground so they look like they were always there. One or two good ones can anchor a whole bed.

items.title: Pea gravel
items.body: Small, smooth stone for tight utility spots. One customer had it laid behind his garage as part of a full yard redo.

blocks.title: Stone for the spots, **mulch for the plants.**
blocks.intro: We install both, so we have no reason to push one. University of Minnesota Extension says organic [mulch](/mulching/) is generally favored in gardens and landscapes, and that stone does not add organic material to the soil. Stone makes sense where planting is light and you would rather not top up a bed every year.

blocks.title: A stone bed gets built from the ground up.

steps.title: Clear
steps.body: Old mulch, weeds and tired plants come out first, because stone laid over old mulch just gives weeds something to grow in. How the debris leaves goes on your estimate.

steps.title: Shape
steps.body: The ground gets raked and sloped so water runs away from the house, and the outline of the bed gets settled on the ground.

steps.title: Edge
steps.body: Loose stone spreads. A border of [steel edging](/steel-edging/), block or stone keeps it out of the lawn and off the walk.

steps.title: Base
steps.body: The ground gets firmed and smoothed so the stone sits even. Whether fabric goes down depends on the bed.

steps.title: Set
steps.body: Boulders go in first, worked into the ground. Then the stone goes in around them, kept back from tree trunks and the stems of your plants.

blocks.footnote: Stone does not fix a wet yard, it only covers one. If water sits by the house, start with [grading](/yard-grading/).

blocks.title: From side yards to commercial fronts.
St. Clair Shores yards **decide how the stone goes in.**
blocks.intro: St. Clair Shores is home, and one of the towns we work in most. The ground, the lot sizes, the water and the city's stormwater fee all shape how a stone bed gets built here.

items.title: Wet, heavy ground
items.body: Most of the city's soil rates poorly or very poorly drained on USDA maps, and the land is close to flat. Water sits on ground like that unless it is shaped to move, so the slope should be set before any stone goes down.

items.title: Narrow side yards
items.body: Inland lots here can run as small as 6,000 square feet, the city's general zoning minimum, and a tight side yard is hard on grass. A strip of river rock is a tidy fix for it.

items.title: Near the lake and the canals
items.body: Lake St. Clair forms the city's east edge, and 14 miles of canals run through it. The lakefront guide the city posts says to keep compost and mulch away from the water, so stone can suit a bed close to it.

items.title: What goes under the stone
items.body: The city bills stormwater by runoff potential, and hard surface counts far more than pervious ground. A landscaped area over an impervious membrane is not on the pervious list, and gravel that misses the city's requirements counts as hard surface. So a liner that lets water through matters here.

blocks.title: What people say after we leave.

faq.q: Do you install rock and stone in St. Clair Shores?
faq.a: Yes. HD Landscape is based in St. Clair Shores and installs river rock, black stone and boulders here and across Metro Detroit, from [Grosse Pointe](/service-areas/grosse-pointe/) to [Birmingham](/service-areas/birmingham/). Call or text Jake at [(586) 718-8762](tel:+15867188762) for a free estimate.

faq.q: Is rock or mulch better for landscaping?
faq.a: Mulch, around most trees, shrubs and perennials. University of Minnesota Extension says organic mulches are generally favored, and that stone and gravel add no organic material to the soil. Rock makes sense in side yards, along walks and foundations, and anywhere you would rather not add a new layer each year. We install both.

faq.q: How do you place boulders so they look natural?
faq.a: Partly in the ground, with the good face turned out. A boulder sitting on top of the soil looks like it fell off a truck. One or two good stones usually do more than a row of small ones.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under rock?
faq.a: Sometimes. Fabric can keep stone from sinking into the soil, especially in a bed with no plants. It is not a permanent weed stop: University of Illinois Extension says it suppresses weeds for only a couple of years and restricts water and air moving through the soil, so it takes care around plants. In St. Clair Shores, a liner that stops water can also change how that area counts toward the stormwater fee. Ask Jake which way he would go on your bed.

faq.q: Will weeds grow through river rock?
faq.a: Some will. University of Illinois Extension says deep stone can hold weeds back in the short term, but weed seeds and soil blow in, and those weeds can be hard to control. Clearing the bed first helps, and a little pulling each season keeps it clean. We can handle that with [weeding](/weeding/) or [monthly maintenance](/monthly-landscape-maintenance/).

faq.q: How deep should landscape rock be?
faq.a: Deep enough to hide the ground, usually a few inches. Small stone covers well in a thinner layer and big river rock needs more, so the right depth comes down to the stone you pick. We work it out at the estimate, so the bed gets what it needs and no more.

faq.q: Can rock go right up against my house?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the ground under it slopes away from the house. Stone does not move water, so a bad grade stays a bad grade under a nice looking bed. If the slope runs the wrong way, [yard grading](/yard-grading/) comes first.

faq.q: Can you put stone around trees?
faq.a: Yes, kept back from the trunk. University of Minnesota Extension says stone and gravel are best for walkways and spots where you do not want anything to grow, and it calls for a 6 inch mulch free ring around a trunk. For trees, a ring of [mulch](/mulching/) is usually the better choice.

faq.q: Can you replace old mulch or gravel with new stone?
faq.a: Yes. The old material should come out first, because stone laid over old mulch gives weeds something to root in. Then the bed gets shaped, edged and filled with new stone. Stone is harder to change than mulch, so take your time on the color.

faq.q: How long does a rock or stone job take?
faq.a: Often one day where the scope allows. Large beds, a lot of boulders or tight access can take longer. One customer had his yard gutted and leveled, with new sod, pea gravel and new plants, and wrote that it was done in one day.

faq.q: What time of year can you install rock and stone?
faq.a: Spring through fall, whenever the ground is workable. Stone can go in during the heat of summer without the watering worries a new planting has, so it is an easy job to fit in when the rest of the yard is busy.

faq.q: How much does rock and stone installation cost?
faq.a: The price comes down to the size of the bed, the stone you choose, how much has to come out first and how easy the spot is to reach, and Jake needs to see it to put a number on it. The estimate is free, and you can go through it line by line. A stone bed skips the yearly layer, which is worth weighing against mulch.

summary.title: Most of the work goes in before the stone does.
